page: Vultr vhf-4c-16gb is a virtual machine instance within the High Frequency Compute family. It is configured with 4 shared vCPUs mapped to 2 physical Intel cores using 2 threads per core, operating at a clock speed of 2.0 GHz. The system includes 16.0 GB of system memory, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. Local storage is bundled with a 384 GB NVMe SSD, and the network configuration includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU hardware is present on this instance.

Benchmark data reveals average performance across several single-core and localized memory operations. The instance achieved a stress-ng single-core CPU score of 2411.16 and a multi-core score of 8740.87, both placing in the middle 50% tier. Small-block cached memory read bandwidth is measured at 497.33 GB/sec. However, performance degrades significantly under larger workloads. Large-block uncached memory read and write bandwidths drop to weak levels of 35.47 GB/sec and 17.49 GB/sec, respectively. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression and software compilation with clang also fall into the bottom 25% performance tier.

Given the shared CPU allocation and the contrast between average single-core performance and weak multi-core scaling, this instance is best suited for lightweight general-purpose workloads. It performs adequately for Redis SET operations, reaching 6.0 million operations per second, and basic text processing. However, it is less optimal for intensive database operations, static web serving, or large-scale LLM inference, where benchmarks show weak to poor throughput. From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the inclusion of a 384 GB NVMe SSD provides a high storage-to-compute ratio, making it a viable option for budget-conscious applications requiring fast local storage but moderate CPU utilization.
description: The Vultr vhf-4c-16gb is an x86_64 virtual server from the High Frequency Compute family, featuring 4 shared Intel vCPUs, 16.0 GB of RAM, and a bundled 384 GB NVMe SSD. Operating at 2.0 GHz, its hardware profile delivers average single-core performance, as evidenced by a Geekbench single-core score of 1471.0 and a Passmark CPU score of 7697.28. However, the shared CPU architecture and memory bandwidth limitations present clear tradeoffs, with weak performance in large-block memory transfers, software compilation, and database operations. While it excels at localized tasks like Redis SET operations, it is less suited for heavy multi-threaded processing or high-throughput web serving. This instance is best utilized for general-purpose workloads, lightweight application hosting, and development environments requiring fast local NVMe storage on a budget-friendly resource allocation.
